utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Have the accused brought in, please, and we will resume our work. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, your Honours. Good afternoon, good afternoon, counsel. The next witness is a protected witness who will be having face distortion and pseudonym. I am informed the next letters are DD. I will refer to the witness as Witness DD. In summary, Witness DD is a 44-year-old Bosnian Muslim who in April 1993 lived in the municipality of Kiseljak in the village of Hercezi. If we have the ELMO illuminated, I put the map on the ELMO and point out the location, the location of the village of Hercezi. It is not marked in orange, Mr. President, but the tip of the pointer points to the actual village itself. Mr. President, and your Honours, Witness DD's testimony will describe the take-over of the village of Hercezi by the HVO. He will describe in the ensuing months that the Bosnian Muslims were permitted to remain in the village, but were essentially under close guard and scrutiny. They had to register, for example, every day with the HVO. During the time he spent in the village after the take-over of the village, which was in April of 1993, he and others in the village were forced to do work by the HVO and that work included the digging of trenches at front-line positions. Ultimately, Mr. President, on approximately 6th September, the HVO came to his village and informed Witness DD and other Muslims who remained in the village that they would be exchanged. They were then taken out of the village and taken to the village of Rotilj. The Witness DD remained in Rotilj until 20th September 1993 and part of his testimony will be to describe to your Honours what happened to him and to the others in the village of Rotilj. He will testify, for example, that in the village of Rotilj, he and other Muslim civilians were taken to front-line positions and had to dig trenches. He will testify that shortly after arriving in Rotilj he was taken to dig trenches at a location near his village and the mosque, which had been intact when he left the village, had been burned down. He will point out in one exhibit the mosque and the various buildings that are attached to the mosque and will describe the destruction of the mosque. On 20th September, he will testify that he was taken to the Kiseljak army barracks in Kiseljak, where he remained for approximately 10 days. While he was there he was beaten, he was robbed and he was forced to dig trenches. He will testify that other Muslim civilians as well had the same experiences during those 10 days he was at the Kiseljak army barracks. He will then testify, Mr. President, that on or about 30th September 1993, he and the Muslim civilians who were in the Kiseljak army barracks were taken to Kresevo, where they remained for approximately one month, essentially as forced labourers. During that month he will describe what happened to him and the other Muslim civilians. He will testify that they were forced on a daily basis to engage in strenuous forced labour, digging trenches and the like. He remained there until approximately 30th October 1993. While there, he will testify that he saw a group of soldiers engage in front-line activities with the HVO. Those soldiers were described by him as the "Maturice". On 30th October, Mr. President, he will testify that he was transferred back -- he and other Muslims were transferred back to the Kiseljak army barracks, where again he was incarcerated, and he will describe the conditions to your Honours. Those conditions include forced labour, trench digging and, ultimately, he was wounded himself on the front-lines on November 18th 1993, while digging trenches. He will testify that he received a serious wound on his back, that he was then transferred from the location where he was digging trenches ultimately back to the Kiseljak army barracks and on that same day taken to Rotilj where he remained until 14th January 1994. He will describe the conditions again on the second visit to Rotilj, this time the visit between November 18th 1993 and 14th January 1994. Those conditions will include description of the HVO coming to the village, rounding up Muslim civilians and taking them to engage in forced labour. Mr. President, his testimony will relate to Count 1 of the indictment, persecution, paragraphs 6.3 to paragraph 7; Count 14 of the indictment, paragraph 11, and counts 15 through 20, paragraphs 12 through 16. That concludes my opening remarks, Mr. President and your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. In order to summarise things and to make things shorter so that we are not going to get lost in all kinds of details, there are four essential points: there is the taking of the village, the period from 6th November to 13th September 1993, which includes the episode in which the exchange took place; there is the period of 20th September to 30th October 1993, at the Kiseljak barracks; then the forced labour period, in Kresevo, if I have that right, and lastly there is a fourth period from the time he was wounded in 1993 and 4th January 1994. Try to be as succinct as possible when you are discussing these essential points, Mr. Prosecutor. Now, let us have Witness DD brought in. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will call you "Witness DD" because you are being covered by protective measures. The Registrar is going to give you a paper on which your name and first name appears, but do not say them. Simply verify that this is you. (Handed).

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now the Registrar is going to give you the oath, that is your solemn declaration. Remain seated and read it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I begin?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You are going to testify at the request of the Prosecutor in the trial being conducted against General Blaskic, who is here in the courtroom. The Prosecutor gave us a summary of the essential points of your testimony. You will speak freely about the points which were pointed out as -- which the Prosecutor indicated as the most important. After several preliminary questions, in blocks of facts or events, you will testify freely. Mr. Prosecutor, you may begin. We will sit for about an hour, or one hour and 15 minutes. WITNESS DD

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me ask you some preliminary questions, Witness DD. Are you a Bosnian citizen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you a Muslim by faith?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In April of 1993, did you live in the Kiseljak municipality, in the village of Hercezi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In April of 1993, were you a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On 18th April 1993, did the HVO occupy the village of Hercezi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I would like to have you testify about certain events in blocks. The first area I would like you to testify about, Witness DD, is from the time of the take-over of your village by the HVO on 18th April 1993 until your ultimate removal from the village on 6th September 1993. Could you describe to the judges the events relating to the take-over and the events that ensued in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the morning of the 18th April 1993, the neighbouring villages were attacked by HVO units. I was surprised that morning because I did not expect anything. I expected -- I thought it was some kind of celebration, something to do with Easter. Then I asked my neighbours what it was. They, too, were surprised. They probably knew what was happening and said "something is wrong". Then we saw the neighbouring villages that were exposed to battle; houses were set on fire. This did not happen in my village, as there was no resistance. We had surrendered what weapons we had, hunting weapons, so that my village was not torched and there was no fighting in my village. On 20th April, during the day, all the weapons were surrendered so that we men spent the evening at our neighbour's house and all night at our neighbours who were Croats, together with the commander, Vucic Pero, known as "Madzar". They were kind to us, they gave us food, dinner, et cetera, so there were no problems, though we felt embarrassed that this had happened and we felt humiliated and offended, et cetera. From 20th April on, we had to report daily. At the edge of my village, there was Radimir Tola, known as Mladen, and his sister Ana kept a record of presence. This reporting had to be done just in case anybody should decide to try and escape, so that they knew that we were all there. After that, we were allowed to work in the field, but not to move away. This went on for about two and a half or three months and then, in August, for a time, we had to dig trenches. Our commander, Pero, known as "Madzar", told us that we should clear the road and to do something because he had orders to force us to do labour. So we cleaned away the road for a couple of days but later on we had to go and dig trenches in the area behind the village of Mr.akovi, a place called Hurije. While digging trenches our neighbours, Croats, were on the front-lines of defence. They treated us fairly, they helped us dig. We had lunch in Stojan's house. After having lunch -- after the Croatian soldiers had lunch, we could also eat whenever there was any food. Later, after that, things became more and more difficult. In August the Croatian police, both the military and the civilian, started arresting people and rounding them up and boarding them onto trucks and taking them to the barracks in Kiseljak and some others to the municipality. I hid so that I was not taken on that occasion, but my neighbours were. This lasted until 6th April, when we went to Rotilj --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness DD, you said "6th April", do you mean 6th September 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I made a mistake, I am sorry, the 6th September. The 6th September. One day -- or rather I did not dig trenches that day because my daughter was going to be exchanged. Seeing her off for the exchange, blue police car together with the military police came and they told us we were all going to be exchanged, so we went to our homes, escorted by the military police. We were given five minutes to get ready and to wait for buses. The buses arrived. We got into them and they drove us, under the excuse that they were taking us for exchange. But we were not exchanged straight away, but were taken to the village of Rotilj, at the cafe called Konek. Both us from the village from Hercezi and others. These military policemen who were escorting us, I do not know where they went but we waited there for a couple of hours, men, women and children and the elderly. Then we were told to go to the upper part of the village of Rotilj, and Hodzic Salko and Fadil Topalovic then helped us in putting us up, though I went to stay with my relatives. As you probably know, the lower part of Rotilj, the Muslim houses were burnt, so that we went to the upper part of the village. We were all crowded into houses --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness DD, let me interrupt you there and ask you some questions about what you have testified to thus far. You mentioned that an individual by the name of Pero had received orders that the Muslims had to engage in forced labour. Was Pero a Bosnian Croat and a member of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pero is a Bosnian Croat and he was the commander of an HVO unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you and the other Bosnian Muslims from Hercezi volunteer to do this work? Was this voluntary labour or was it coerced?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Obviously under those conditions, it was forced labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me show you, with the assistance of the usher, Exhibit 273, and ask you if you can identify this exhibit. Mr. President, and your Honours, Exhibit 273 is a map that has eight locations mapped. Attached to it are numbers that -- the identities of locations which he correspond to numbers which are on the map itself. (Handed). Witness DD, did you have an opportunity to mark on Prosecutor's Exhibit 273, the green marks that are found on the exhibit itself, which represent locations where you had to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Answer not translated).

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you also indicate the names associated with each of the numbers found on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, throughout your testimony today, you will be referring to various locations where you were forced to dig trenches. Are all those locations indicated on Prosecutor's Exhibit 273?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The first location that you have testified about is the area of Mr.akovi. You do not have to put it on the ELMO, you can just testify about it. The first location where you had to dig trenches in Mr.akovi, is that location number 1 or location number 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 1, the location of Mr.akovi or, more, precisely, Hurije.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you some questions then relating to your removal from the village of Hercezi on about 6th September 1993. Were all of the Muslim villagers who remained in the village of Hercezi removed by the HVO on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All Muslims from Herceg were taken away that day except for one person who was disabled, and two days later he and his wife was brought as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you left on 6th September what was the condition of the mosque that was in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We passed by bus, by the mosque and it was intact, with the exception of some of the inventory that had been looted from the inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, there appears to be a mis-translation to one of the answers that is given -- apparently it is not a mis-translation. Apparently it is what the witness said. Let me ask you again, Witness DD. The question I asked you was, on 6th September were all the villagers were the village of Hercezi taken away from by the HVO. The answer that shows up on the screen is "all Muslims from Herceg were taken away"; did you mean Hercezi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hercezi, the village of Hercezi with the exception of one man and woman who were transported two days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In respect of the homes that you and the other Muslim residents of Hercezi vacated, on 6th September, what happened to those homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All the houses were intact, except for one, owned by Hasim Turcinovic, which was torched before we left for Rotilj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did anybody move into your houses, the vacated houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Croatian inhabitants from Fojnica moved into our houses immediately. This was organised by Stanic Ivica, known as Anica, and Oris Ljube from Fojnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: To your knowledge, do the Croats who moved into your houses still live in your houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are still living there, though there has been some movement. Some from returned to Fojnica. Then after that some houses were burnt and the mosque was also set fire to after we left to Rotilj, or rather the minaret was mined later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let us talk about your stay in Rotilj between 6th September and 20th September 1993. Can you tell the judges about the conditions that you and the other Muslims found in the village, in Rotilj when you arrived on 6th September 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The people in front of the hotel moved to the upper part of the village. With great difficulty they were put up. There were so many people that it was impossible to find accommodation for all of them. Some were in a religious building and others in houses abandoned by that date. Of course we were all surrounded in that village. There were soldiers from HV -- HVO soldiers from Kakanj living above the village. They would shoot when they were drunk. Then there were artillery pieces above the village too. In the lower part of the village there was a checkpoint with two guards on duty round the clock. Then the village was toured by Juro Tuka, an elderly man over 60, who was armed with a rifle, and he could not be a military conscript, allegedly to look after the safety of the inhabitants. It was impossible for us to move to Kiseljak to get food, to see a doctor and that sort of thing, because the conflict had already started. People were terrified and they realised what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you were in Rotilj, did you and other Muslim male civilians have to go to dig trenches because the HVO took you to those locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For six or seven days, we did not go to dig trenches, until some kind of a record was made. The local people went to other locations, whereas we, from Herceg were sent to Mr.akovi again, to the region number 2, as marked on this map. That was where the defence lines were held by people from Visnjica, Dolat and Fojnica. That is troops of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when you went to this location, Mr.akovi, did you have an opportunity to pass the mosque in the village of Hercezi and could you describe to the judges the condition of the mosque as you saw it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we passed by the mosque in a small van, a TAM van, the mosque was on fire. We just saw that it had been set on fire. We could not see anything else. The minaret was still there. It had not been blown up yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, if we could place Exhibit 68 on the screen, I am particularly interested in a single photograph, 689, in Exhibit 68, please. (Handed). If you place that on the ELMO, please, usher. Thank you. Witness DD, there appears to be two main structures in that particular photograph. First of all, do you recognise what that photograph represents and could you tell the judges what that is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This photograph shows the mosque. The western entrance, the eastern part of the mosque with the premises downstairs where the dead people would be bathed and the prayers done. To the right was the minaret. This is the house where the hodza lived. In the ground floor was a classroom for children and this was a small premise where the tools for digging tombs were held. Here there is a shed and wood was held there. Over here was green iron gate and there was a wire fence around it. (Indicating on photograph). There was a basin with water here and three tombs were dug here where Muslim soldiers, if you like to call them that, were buried in exchange for fighters of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, usher. I am finished with that particular exhibit. Now, Witness DD, I would like to turn your attention to your stay in the Kiseljak barracks, between 20th September 1993 and approximately 30th September 1993. Before you start your testimony, if I could show you the Prosecutor's next exhibit, which is Exhibit 274, and ask that that be placed on the ELMO. Mr. President and your Honours, Exhibit 274 is an enlargement of a previously admitted exhibit, Exhibit 75, it has three locations marked on it. The accompanying legend identifies those locations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Around 20th April, the military police came to fetch me and one of my relatives and they took us to the barracks in Kiseljak. There they put us up --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness DD -- let me interrupt you for a second. Let me ask you, first of all, if you can see the exhibit that is placed on the ELMO. There are three numbers and three circles on that particular exhibit. Did you indicate these locations to me and do I have these locations marked on this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you tell the judges, starting with number 1, what number 1 is, what number 2 is and what number 3 is on this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 1 is the entrance gate and a board with the words "barracks", the word "kasana" which was replaced with the word "vojane" and the chequer board flag. This was the guard house where the guards used to be. This was a road, a parking place and this was the pavilion or the place where the prisoners were held. This was the command building. The part where we were held, the prisoners, there was a corridor, a small office, with a commander and the other interrogators who questioned the prisoners. To the left was a room where Dore, the interrogator, used to work. To the right was a larger room, it was dark, where I was placed for the first time, where I found the other prisoners and here there was another smaller room. Later on we were moved to this room. Next to it was another small room for the cleaning of weapons and another small room known as the marsana, for the police -- marsana.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Number 3 is where you were detained, the building in which you were detained; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is number 2 on this particular exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 2 is the command building, probably where the command of the HVO unit, Fociceljak, was accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you please tell the judges in your own words about the conditions in the Kiseljak army barracks for you and the other Muslim detainees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When entering or going out of the cell, the room, we had to have our head bowed and our hands on our back, in a straight line, one by one. The same applied when we went to do labour, or when we were lined up in the hall. In one of these rooms there were about 55 of us prisoners. Inside we had plastic containers and plastic bottles for urination because we had no chance of going outside except when we went to work and in the morning we would be given one minute to defecate. Then a policeman from near Travnik would mistreat individual prisoners. We slept on blankets on the floor and we were given one blanket to two or three of us as covers. The room was over-crowded because it was about four by five metres in size. Of course, we were beaten. I would not say that all the prisoners were beaten, but most of them were and I know of some, and among them I was one. A few days later, after being interrogated by Miro Biletic, the prison warden, his father was Ivo, he was born in 1958, he interrogated me, together with two other policemen, but they did not beat me. The second night, I was called by the soldier on duty of the HVO and that evening I was beaten by the policeman, the military policeman of the HVO, Spreco, who came from Plakarevo, near Travnik. Before beating me, he told me to take out everything I had in my pocket, to take off my watch and I had 820 German Marks and I had to give them to him. He beat me for about 15 minutes and he would say to me -- he would suggest to me that we should have a boxing match. Of course, I did not dare say anything and he would continue beating me, saying -- repeating the same words: "Where is your pistol?". After this beating the policeman took me out again and asked me to take off my leather jacket for them to use and then they would give it back to me. They never did and all I had on was a T-shirt. A couple of days later, or to be more precise, on 29th September, they beat me in this marsana. I was beaten by five military policemen of the HVO. Miro Biletic was behind the door. He hit me with a stick and the rest of them with their boots. It is interesting that they did not hit me on my legs or my head but only in the ribs, my stomach, the kidney area and above the kidneys, in my back. After this beating, which lasted for about 21 to 30 minutes, Miro Biletic winked and said: "Let him go, that is enough". Before that beating I had to take off a sweatshirt that I had found and then he wound the sweatshirt round my head and took me out. During the beating itself, a policeman was standing at the door with lights pointing into my eyes, spotlights. I did not dare ask anything, then a policeman came and said: "Get up and put your hands against the wall." We stood there for about 15 minutes. They did not do anything. Then we could put our hands down. In addition to Miro, there was this policeman Spreco, Ivo Medic, Marinko, 1962 from Zavraje, Frankovic Zeljo. After that, on the 29th in the night, to the 30th, about four o'clock, we were transferred in a Zastava vehicle to Kresevo to dig trenches in the Mehurisce area --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there before we get to Kresevo. Let me ask you some clarifying questions: while you were at the Kiseljak barracks during the time period of 20th to 30th September 1993, did you have to dig trenches, and if so, can you tell the judges where you dug the trenches, how many people dug the trenches, whether they were civilians, whether they were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the prison, in Kiseljak, we were all civilians. Allegedly there was another room where the BiH army soldiers who had been captured were detained. I did not see this. Of course, we were forced to dig trenches and to engage in other forced labour in addition to trenches, even though all the trenches were right on the front-line. Usually a commander would come from one of the regions, asking for so many prisoners to dig trenches. Our names would be called out. We would get into the small TAM van or a Zastava vehicle. The driver or the escort or the commander or a policeman would close the doors and then a small vehicle would follow just in case anyone tried to escape. The same applied on the way back. As far as food is concerned, in Kiseljak, itself, the rule was that the people digging trenches were given some food on the spot, whereas those who did not -- and they were the elderly and the sick -- were not given food. I must point out that Slavko Biletic, a policeman from Kakanj, and Miro Colic would sometimes find some food for us, some bread and some Italian tins or Australian beans and they would give them to us. Indeed, they protected us as much as they could and I want to mention them for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness DD, would you go on a daily basis to the front-lines and then return the same day from trench digging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went on a daily basis, except when there was fighting, when we did other kind of work. Sometimes we stayed for several days, such as Brezova Kosa, Basino Brdo in the Otigojce region in Kresevo, the region of the enterprise barrack.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when you were taken out of building 3 and loaded into small vehicles, where were those vehicles parked? Were they parked between the commander's headquarters which is number 2, and the barracks in which you were housed, which is number 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the access road to building number 3 and in the direction of building number 2, which is the command building, it depended.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You were loaded up -- you and the other Muslims who were taken to go dig trenches, you were loaded into vans that were parked between building 2 and building 3; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. About 30 to 50 metres away -- the buildings were about 30 to 50 metres apart and a vehicle would come up to, say, the administration building.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there any attempt, by the people who were taking you to dig trenches, to conceal you and the other Muslim prisoners who were being taken from the line of sight from the command building? Were they trying to hide you from the commanders in the building in number 2?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there any attempt by the people who took you and the other Muslims to dig trenches to conceal you from view from the people who were in the commanders' building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know anything about that. I actually do not understand, so I do not know. I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me try to approach the question in a different way: when you were loaded into the vans, could the people who were in the building number 2 see the people who were being loaded into the vans?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, now I understood. Yes, of course, you could see it because it was not any great distance. Of course you could see it and we did see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The same is true when you returned from the trenches, you were unloaded in the same location; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we would usually go there in the morning and we would come back in the evening. Sometimes it was -- sometimes it would already be dark when we came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness DD, if you could just point to the locations on Exhibit 273 where you and the other Muslims were taken to dig trenches during that time frame we are talking about. How many locations were you taken to dig trenches and which ones are they on Prosecutor's Exhibit 273?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prisoners were taken to various places. I was, again, taken to the sector marked with "3" towards Crvena Stijena, Palesko Brdo and in 3 Palesko Brdo in the direction of Visoko. I was also taken to the sector number 8, Brezova Kosa. Sector 4, that is Brajkovici, above the church towards Gunovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness DD, let me ask you a couple more questions. You said that your watch was stolen and a little over 800 Deutschmarks was taken from you. Was either the watch or money returned to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were valuables from other Muslim civilians who were housed in the Kiseljak army barracks also taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard people spoke about it, but I never saw anything with my own eyes, so I cannot speak to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let us turn now to your experiences in Kresevo. Were you taken to Kresevo on or about 30th September 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken to Kresevo in the morning hours over there in front of a pool, that is the motel in Kresevo. From there we went to Mehurisce and Svinjarevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who took you to Kresevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were taken by the HVO soldiers together with the police and together with me was also the mining engineer, Vid, who was also in charge of construction of the building of fragmentation mines. He worked in the company called Celik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you describe to the judges your experiences during the month when you were in Kresevo? Could you do that succinctly, please? Your description is to describe the conditions, the type of food you received, what you were forced to do. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We slept in the barrack hall. I think about 34 of us, something around that number, came up there and we found there some other prisoners from the Kresevo municipality, part of them from Jajce who happened to be there and some from Svinjarevo. Usually in the morning there would be a roll call of sort. Each prisoner who went to work would get a third or a quarter of bread and a pack of margarine and this would be divided between 30/40 to 70 people, it depended. Then we would be passed to Banje or the sector of Tola. From there we would go on foot usually using paths. The engineers of the HVO were just in the process of constructing new roads, so that they could link it up to the HVO positions around Mehurisce.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness DD, you said you found a number of other Muslims at Kresevo in the location where you were brought by the HVO. Approximately how many other Muslims were there and were they civilians or were they soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the Kresevo hall, together with the Kiseljak and Kresevo people, there were about 80 of us. About 60 people went to dig trenches, a few people were sick and some elderly people went to certain villages to deal with the crops. I can also add that there were some miners among the prisoners in this hall. Out in the field we also received some bread, some margarine, sometimes some jam. I also need to add that there was a Nikola from Pirin, who was an elderly man who brought this food for us. Sometimes he would give us some burek or some extra canned food. I would also like to give him credit for that. I would also like to say that we had good tools, they really had good tools for digging, so it was easier for us to dig there --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness DD, approximately how many days did you dig trenches when you were in Kresevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was exactly one month. One part of the civilians -- the prisoners from Kresevo left early, they were there for about 15 days and we stayed exactly one month. So that on the 30th of October, we were returned to the Kiseljak barracks. I would like to add that on 25th October we were, for the first time, registered in Kresevo by the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Moving ahead with this part of your examination, was there sufficient food for you and the other Muslim people forced to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not have enough food, both in quantity and quality, given the kind of work that we did. When we returned from Kresevo to Kiseljak and until I was wounded, I think I lost about 28 kilograms. When I returned to Kiseljak, to the barracks, I had 112 kilograms and when I was released I had 84.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the other Muslims who were forced to dig trenches also suffer extreme weight loss?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, the very fact speaks about it. There was a lot of work and not enough food. After we came back from Kresevo we had some cooked food but it was not very much, it did not have enough fat in it or enough salt.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I want to move through parts of your testimony fairly quickly, Witness DD. While you were at the front-lines at Kresevo, did you see soldiers dressed in black? Can you identify those soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While we were working on the front-lines of the HVO, one day they sensed that there may -- a counterattack may be coming from the BiH army so the reinforcements came and those soldiers were called Maturice. They were of course wearing black uniforms, they had good weapons, they had arm bands and insignia of the HVO. At the time the positions were being fortified and I do not know who did this, the commander's name, but he took us with him to a burnt house which belonged to somebody called Stanic. We made fire there because it was cold and I really would like to salute this commander because he saved us that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness DD, can you tell us, in respect of Prosecutor's Exhibit 273, where was it that you were forced to dig trenches around Kresevo? Which number is it on Exhibit 273? Just point to the number and tell us which one it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Number 5, this was the sector, Mehurisce, Cimburov Brijeg, and above Pirin. It was called -- above Pirin, around there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. Witness DD --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What number is that, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Number 5, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness DD, I would like you to tell the judges about your experiences once you returned from Kresevo to the Kiseljak army barracks, you returned on or about the 30th October and you remained there until the 18th November 1993, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the judges about your experiences at the Kiseljak army barracks during that time frame?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we returned to the Kiseljak barracks, we found in the room about 50 prisoners. That means that five of them had been released. We again went to dig trenches in the sector of Brezova Kosa. Then Brajkovici-Oglavac. We spent two days at that but there were combat operations going there so we did not dig. We spent the night there and returned to Kiseljak. We were in Kiseljak for a couple of days because there were combat operations going on in Jasikovac and the Basino Brdo sector and on the 15th November we were transferred together with some other people who were in the municipal building to the Otigosce sector and from there to dig trenches in Jasikovac and Basino Brdo. I remained there for about three days. On the 18th November, an attack was launched by the HVO units and I was wounded, together with another two prisoners. From there, with another HVO soldier, I was transferred to or received first aid. With this mining engineer, Vid, I was transferred to the Otigosce sector. I was examined and it was determined that there was a bullet in my right-hand side. I stayed there for a couple of hours and then went to war hospital in Kiseljak. I was properly examined. Everything was done properly and everything was all right and I then asked Vlado Markovic, who has since died, and his son to take us to the infirmary in the barracks and I asked this man, Frankovic, for some pills. He did not give them to me, but Dr Vujica gave them to me and then he ordered this driver to take me and my colleague back to a room and we stayed there for another couple of hours and later two military policemen took me in a police vehicle to the Rotilj village and there I was, until 14th January 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you briefly some questions about your stay in the Kiseljak barracks until 18th November 1993. You indicated that you and other Muslims had to go dig trenches. Just very briefly, if you could point out on Prosecutor's Exhibit 273 the various locations. Identify them by number, where you and the other Muslims were taken to dig trenches. Just identify them by number.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to the sector number 8, Brezova Kosa, number 6, Brijkovic, but we did not dig there and Basino Brdo, the sector where I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How many times did you go to Brezova Kosa, which is number 8?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went once but we stayed there for five or six days. One group stayed there and one group returned. We spent the night in the house of a person called Zlatko, who moved from Kakanj and he was commander of this sector, Lukic, Brezova Kosa. We were in a basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you returned from the area of Kresevo to the Kiseljak barracks, you said you saw approximately 50 people in building number 3, which is the barracks. Could you tell me, were those all Muslims and were they civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were all Muslims civilians. Among them was also a young Muslim man, Jasmin Uzunovic, who was told to provoke the prisoners, because he was not mentally healthy. I can also add that before and after my stay at Kresevo in Kiseljak there were two French men, but Muslims. They went to be exchanged and I do not know when it was, after we returned from one of these labour stints they were gone. They were also beaten a lot. Why, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when you were wounded on the 18th November, 1993, you were taken the same day to Rotilj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was the bullet that wounded you ever removed from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is still in my body, and I submit as proof the referral of the doctor there received and also I can confirm it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: After you were taken to Rotilj on the 18th November you remained there until -- I believe you testified 14th January 1994. Could you please describe to the judges the conditions you found in Rotilj when you arrived on the 18th November and the conditions that existed through the 14th January 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In addition to Rotilj also being a camp, it was much easier for me there than in the barracks. So, I recuperated a little. I got better food so that I could recover fully. There was also a ban on movement, you could not go anywhere. There was private exchanging going on. I waited for about 40 days to be privately exchanged before I went. Money did not mean much there. When I came back from -- when I -- when I left the barracks a number of people were exchanged, and so we waited almost every night for someone to be privately exchanged. I was privately exchanged on 14th January 1994. Of course, people were afraid of robberies and looting. Men were afraid of being recaptured and taken to dig trenches again. They would be taken to do other types of labour. At one point a policeman came to where I was staying. He said, "we need two people to go to dig trenches because two elderly men refuse because they are too weak." I showed him my certificate showing that I was wounded, then he was decent with me and he let me alone. So it was very difficult. I received some humanitarian aid during this period. Sometimes Dr Pero would come to Rotilj. He would bring some medicine for people who were sick, but it was not normal by any stretch of the imagination. We were surrounded. There were guards, there was a gate you could pass through then. You did not dare, you were afraid you would be taken to dig trenches or do other type of labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you were there during the last part of your captivity, up until 14th January 1994, was it quite a normal occurrence that the HVO would come in and select men to take to dig trenches and perform other forms of forced labour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was, either during the day or towards the evening, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness DD. Mr. President and your Honours, I would move to introduce Prosecutor's Exhibits 273 and 274 into evidence. I have concluded my examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. I note that you absolutely respected the summary that you announced and we judges congratulate you. Mr. Nobilo, in the cross-examination, I am sure that you have some questions. Mr. Nobilo is General Blaskic's Defence attorney. He is going to ask you some questions now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Good evening. You said on 18th April 1993 the HVO took the village; did they attack or did they just come to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no armed conflict in our village. They just took control of the territory and when we surrendered these hunting weapons we offered no resistance. There was no fighting there, unlike Visnjica, Gomlonica, Svinjarevo villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In these villages, where people did not surrender their weapons, how much shooting and when did you hear the shooting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a couple of days and for up to a month later you could hear sporadic fire. I could not pinpoint the locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that you had to report in every day. Did this mean men, or women and children as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only the able-bodied men had to report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was this changed later and it was less frequent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was also done later, because a couple of people fled to the territory of the BiH army or were exchanged so it was made more frequent and then it was then again relaxed later, because it was also more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In the area of Hurije where you dug trenches, how far is that from your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is about two to two and a half kilometres from my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Does that mean that the front-line was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and then it moved towards Plocari up to the mosque and to Plandiste.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Does that mean that it kept coming closer to your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the HVO kept advancing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you dug, did you dig fox-holes, dug-outs, trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was the fortification of the front-lines. It was the trenches and sometimes dug-outs and it was -- they would be covered with some light construction materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you ask that your daughter be exchanged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I did not know that, some of my relatives did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you ask for an exchange -- did you ask UNPROFOR for exchange?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: do not need to speak any names before your protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So, the HVO -- the authorities did not allow you to leave even though you wanted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When did you see the mosque as being destroyed, what month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was in the month of September, sometime around six to seven days after my departure for Rotilj. So that would mean on the 13th or 14th September.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: At that time you were not present there, you do not know who destroyed it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not. I just passed by there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The people who moved into your village, why did they leave their own residences? Do you know under what circumstances they left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I learned when I came to Rotilj, I learned that. They were in the same situation as we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In other words, the army drove them out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many people from Fojnica came to the Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know really, I had no way of finding out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you know in January/February of 1993, from Bilalovac and the surrounding villages a number of Croatian refugees came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: From Bilalovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kacuni and the surrounding villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And where did they come; to the Kiseljak municipality territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you arrived in Rotilj, was there some fence there, like a real camp has?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there was no fence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were there any patrols of armed soldiers who walked around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some in the upper part of the village, the soldiers from Kakanj, who would sometimes get drunk and shoot. Those were the soldiers who lived here, and down at the entrance where this Muslim population was, so there was a gate there so you could not pass on the main road. Maybe there were some other points which I did not see.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Except for the people who were at that gate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was more like a ramp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Okay, a ramp or checkpoint. How many were they there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were mostly two people, sometimes one even. When I would pass from digging trenches I would just see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Except for those one or two at the ramp and the elderly man of 60 who guarded you, were there any other soldiers there, in the sense that they worked in protecting you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I do not know. I did not see any.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Those at the ramp, did you also feel them as being there for your own protection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe, but I do not know that, maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did Caritas bring in their trucks food from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, UNHCR did and Caritas did and that was positive too. Even the priest from Gromiljak also sent some.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was this a regular thing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not regular, but he did it for his own parishioners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, that was the priest. What about Caritas, did they ship it regularly every month?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that. I was not there all the time. When I was wounded, I know that the UNHCR sent something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could we say that during the war there was more food in Rotilj than elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be honest with you, given the famine and the food that was available in what the UNHCR kept bringing and everything else, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So was there more in Rotilj than elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I was in Rotilj --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But you said that elsewhere there was famine; was there any famine in Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, you could not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When the commander -- did the commander from Rotilj protect you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To be honest with you, I do not even know even know who the commander in Rotilj was. I was recovering there. I was lying, I did not move around so I cannot tell you much about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Why were you imprisoned? Did you do something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not do anything. There was one interrogation. I had hunting weapons which I surrendered, but I had permits for it. The first question they asked me in Kiseljak, they asked me what were my relations with my neighbour, Adranija. I said I was fine with him. Then they asked me where was his weapons, I said I did not know. Then they asked me whether I took part in any attacks and I said I had no ideas over that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So those were some accusations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, those were questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would just like to remind you in your statement which you gave previously, on page number 5, in the second paragraph from the top, you said that the commander of the camp was trying to protect you, that is to prevent any crimes against you, some robberies, loot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean in the Kresevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: No, in Rotilj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, in Rotilj. You mean the elderly man who walked around the village?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tuka is his name. He had that role because he wanted to protect us from some kind of attack, mistreatment or from being looted and sometimes he would come and he let us know about -- if anything happened, so he did try to do something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I believe that this was not entered right in the in the transcript; you were wounded during the attack of the BiH army on 18th November?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the HVO pushed the line towards Fojnica and they were fortifying the lines and we -- prisoners were digging at the time and then the BiH army counterattacked and that is when I was wounded, and I was wounded by the BiH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You told the judges that you were privately exchanged. What does that mean? That was without the knowledge of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was without the HVO authority knowledge, because a man came to Rotilj and he said: "Get ready, we are going to get exchanged". So we got ready, there was nine of us altogether, we went up to Tusnjic. We came up there and we waited until this was sorted out. I do not know how and what was done. There were four people from Kakanj, four Croatians, a woman, a man and I think two children. Before that, a man was sent to Kiseljak with a list and the HVO units let him through. He was going to go to Kiseljak and ask for these people, so this private exchange took place without any commissions, knowledge or UNHCR or people who were involved in this. So we were exchanged in that way and it was all done fairly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was this for money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was not done for money, even though my father and my younger daughter were exchanged for money.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But the authorities did not know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You were in Hercezi, you dug in many different locations. You were in the Kiseljak barracks in Fojnica, in Rotilj, in all these places; did you ever see Colonel Blaskic in any of those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not ever, even though he is my neighbour. I only saw him on BH television with the former General, Sefer Halilovic and some others.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did anybody refer to him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, that is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness DD. I just wanted to have a clarification. When you spoke of the mosque, when you came back and the mosque was destroyed, was there any knowledge about the way it was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The mosque was only set on fire and the roof, sort of, collapsed. Then you could only see some smoke coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Nobody knew who set it on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody knew, nobody could know which has passed by there, but the time will come when this will come out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Were other public places like schools or institutions also damaged and burned down?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not have such structures. During the conflict, no structures were destroyed, but after the mosque, Ganija Havdos, Sahet Meho, Sahet Ahmed, Ranica Cinovic, and Zulko and Hasim Turcinovic houses were all destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: What was particular about these houses? Were they prominent people, were they among the leaders of the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were houses in the upper part of the village and nobody moved in them. Most probably they were looted and later set on fire. Why, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Looted by whom, do they know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croatian population from the village of Markovi and Lug.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: By other neighbours or by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croatian neighbours, civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Just one question. It is about these same houses which were burned down. You mentioned a number of names of owners. Who were these owners; were they Croats or Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was speaking of these owners, I referred to all of them as Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness DD, you were taken care of by the Croats -- at least by the Bosnian Croats -- when you were in Rotilj. How do you explain that? You had been mistreated for weeks, for months, you are wounded -- that is, you were wounded by Bosnian Army troops, and yet you were well treated, well taken care of. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the midst of some many atrocities that were committed, perhaps not so much precaution was taken. People who helped me and who examined me and offered me care all knew me and they were all fair to me. I have to give them credit. I have to tell the court how it was. In fact, I can say that they did not distinguish between me and another wounded HVO soldier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Your testimony is complete. The International Criminal Tribunal thanks you for having come to The Hague. Please do not move for the time being. We will suspend our work, it is now 6.45. We will resume on 16th March, subject to anything the Registrar would like to say. I would like to say that we have heard five witnesses in six calendar days, according to the Registrar. For the Prosecution there are about 30 calendar days left; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Full days, that is for the examination and cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: There is a lot of work to be done yet, not only as regards examination of the witnesses but also as regards precision and succinctness. Thank you very much. We will see one another again on 16th March. (6.45 pm)
